chapter.title: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery
chapter.description: Fifteen recurring IELTS domains. Each topic contains ten academic nouns, ten precise verbs, ten collocations/adjectives, five formal Task 2 collocations, five Speaking idioms/expressions, and three exercises. The batch answer keys retain the worked solutions and model speaking responses.

blocks.title: Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 1 of 3)
blocks.content:
Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 1 of 3)
The fifteen domains in this chapter are the topics IELTS returns to again and again. Whatever
the exact question, your Task 2 essay and your Speaking answers will draw on this vocabulary.
Each topic gives you a complete bundle: ten academic nouns, ten precise verbs, ten collocations
and adjectives, five formal collocations built for Writing Task 2, and five natural idioms built
for Speaking. The line between the last two matters enormously, and Chapter 5 is devoted to it;
here, simply notice that the formal set is labelled for Writing and the idiom set for Speaking,
and keep them apart.
This batch covers the first five domains: Environment, Education, Technology, Health, and
Crime. Batches 2 and 3 cover the remaining ten. Work each topic, then do its three exercises
before checking the key at the end of the file.
A note on the Bangla glosses: they give the everyday meaning of each academic noun so the
term is anchored to something you already know. Do not translate word for word into your
essays; use the English term in its natural collocation.

blocks.title: Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 2 of 3)
blocks.content:
Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 2 of 3)
This batch covers domains six to ten: Globalisation and Cultural Assimilation, Urbanisation and
Infrastructure, Business and Economy, Arts and Heritage, and Media and Advertising. The
format is identical to Batch 1. Work each topic, then complete its three exercises before
checking the key at the end of the file. Keep the formal Task 2 collocations and the Speaking
idioms apart in your mind; the strict register rule that governs them is the whole subject of
Chapter 5.

blocks.title: Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 3 of 3)
blocks.content:
Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 3 of 3)
This final batch covers the last five domains: Government Governance and Public Spending,
Transportation and Mobility, Youth and Family and Generational Gaps, Scientific Research and
Innovation, and International Tourism and Travel. Complete each topic and its three exercises
before checking the key at the end. With this batch, all fifteen IELTS domains are covered.

blocks.title: Environment and Climate Shift

sections.title: Academic nouns (10)
sections.content:
1.     emission (নিঃসরণ): Industrial emissions are a leading driver of global warming.
2.     deforestation (বন উজাড় ): Widespread deforestation has accelerated the loss of natural
habitats.
3.     biodiversity (জীববৈচিত্র্য): The destruction of wetlands threatens the region’s biodiversity.
4.     ecosystem (বাস্তু তন্ত্র): Even small changes in temperature can disrupt a fragile ecosystem.
5.     degradation (অবক্ষয়): Soil degradation reduces agricultural productivity over time.
6.     sustainability (টেকসইতা): Long-term sustainability must guide national energy policy.
7.     conservation (সংরক্ষণ): The conservation of freshwater resources is now an urgent
priority.
8.     pollutant (দূষক): Vehicle exhaust releases harmful pollutants into the atmosphere.
9.     depletion (নিঃশেষ হওয়া): The depletion of fossil fuels has intensified the search for
alternatives.
10. carbon footprint (কার্বন পদচিহ্ন): Individuals can reduce their carbon footprint by using
public transport.

sections.title: Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
sections.content:
1.  emit (emitted, emitted, emitting): Factories emit large quantities of greenhouse gases.
2.  deplete (depleted, depleted, depleting): Overfishing has depleted marine stocks
worldwide.
3. mitigate (mitigated, mitigated, mitigating): Reforestation can mitigate the effects of
climate change.
4. conserve (conserved, conserved, conserving): Households should conserve water
during the dry season.
5. pollute (polluted, polluted, polluting): Untreated waste continues to pollute major
rivers.
6. degrade (degraded, degraded, degrading): Intensive farming gradually degrades the
soil.
7. offset (offset, offset, offsetting): Companies can offset emissions by funding tree
planting.
8. preserve (preserved, preserved, preserving): Protected areas help preserve endangered
species.
9. exploit (exploited, exploited, exploiting): Nations must stop exploiting natural
resources recklessly.
10. contaminate (contaminated, contaminated, contaminating): Chemical runoff can
contaminate groundwater.

sections.title: Collocations and adjectives (10)
sections.content:
1.  renewable energy: Investment in renewable energy is rising steadily. (Writing)
2.  fossil fuels: We remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. (Writing)
3.  environmentally friendly: Many consumers now prefer environmentally friendly
products. (Speaking and Writing)
4. a pressing environmental concern: Air quality has become a pressing environmental
concern. (Writing)
5. greenhouse gas emissions: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires global
cooperation. (Writing)
6. irreversible damage: Rising sea levels could cause irreversible damage to coastlines.
(Writing)
7. carbon neutral: Several cities aim to become carbon neutral by 2050. (Writing)
8. finite resources: Water and oil are finite resources that must be managed carefully.
(Writing)
9. eco-friendly (Speaking): I try to make eco-friendly choices, like carrying a reusable
bottle. (Speaking)
10. climate change (adjective use, climate-related): Climate-related disasters are becoming
more frequent. (Writing)

sections.title: Formal Task 2 collocations (5)
sections.content:
1.     pose a serious threat to: Rising temperatures pose a serious threat to food security.
2.     at the expense of: Economic growth should not come at the expense of the
environment.
3.     strike a balance between: Governments must strike a balance between development
and conservation.
4.     have a detrimental impact on: Plastic waste has a detrimental impact on marine life.
5.     take collective action: Only collective action can address the climate crisis effectively.

sections.title: Speaking idioms and expressions (5)
sections.content:
1.     a drop in the ocean: Recycling at home helps, but it is a drop in the ocean compared
with industry. (Part 3)
2.     the tip of the iceberg: The visible pollution is just the tip of the iceberg. (Part 3)
3.     go green: More families are trying to go green these days. (Part 1)
4.     weather the storm: Coastal communities have to weather the storm of frequent
flooding. (Part 3)
5.     a breath of fresh air: Escaping to the countryside is a real breath of fresh air. (Part 2)

sections.title: Part B
sections.content:
Exercise 4.1.1 · Vocabulary Match. Match each term (1 to 10) with its meaning (a to j).
1.     emission · 2. biodiversity · 3. depletion · 4. mitigate · 5. sustainability · 6. pollutant · 7. offset
· 8. finite · 9. conservation · 10. degrade
a.     the variety of living things in an area
b.     to reduce the severity of something harmful
c.     a substance that makes air, water, or soil dirty
d.     limited in quantity, not endless
e.     the release of gas or heat into the air
f.     to make something worse in quality over time
g.     the careful protection of natural resources
h.     to balance out a negative amount with a positive action
i.     the state of being able to continue over the long term
j.     the using up or reduction of a resource
Exercise 4.1.2 · Essay Sentence Completion. Complete each Task 2 sentence with a term from
this topic.
1.     Governments must ______ a balance between industrial growth and environmental
protection.
2.     Burning fossil fuels releases harmful ______ into the atmosphere.
3.     Investment in ______ energy is essential if we are to cut emissions.
4.     Deforestation causes ______ damage that cannot be undone.
5.     Individuals can lower their carbon ______ by choosing public transport.
Exercise 4.1.3 · Speaking Simulation Drill. Answer each Part 3 question in two to three
sentences, using at least one target idiom and one collocation.
1.     What can ordinary people do to protect the environment?
2.     Do you think individual effort is enough to solve climate change?
3.     How might cities become more environmentally friendly in the future?

blocks.title: Education and Pedagogy

sections.title: Academic nouns (10)
sections.content:
1.  curriculum (পাঠ্যক্রম): A modern curriculum should balance theory with practical skills.
2.  pedagogy (শিক্ষণবিদ্যা): Effective pedagogy adapts to the needs of individual learners.
3.  literacy (সাক্ষরতা): Improving adult literacy is a key development goal.
4.  assessment (মূল্যায়ন): Continuous assessment reduces the pressure of a single final
exam.
5. enrolment (ভর্তি): University enrolment has risen sharply over the past decade.
6. discipline (শৃঙ্খলা): Self-discipline is essential for successful independent study.
7. attainment (অর্জন): Educational attainment is closely linked to future income.
8. vocation (বৃত্তি): Vocational training prepares students for specific trades.
9. aptitude (দক্ষতা / সহজাত ক্ষমতা): Standardised tests attempt to measure academic
aptitude.
10. scholarship (বৃত্তি / শিক্ষাবৃত্তি): Scholarships enable talented students from poor families to
study.

sections.title: Precise verbs (10)
sections.content:
1.     enrol (enrolled, enrolled, enrolling): Thousands of students enrol in online courses
each year.
2.     acquire (acquired, acquired, acquiring): Children acquire language most easily when
young.
3.     cultivate (cultivated, cultivated, cultivating): Good schools cultivate curiosity, not just
obedience.
4.     assess (assessed, assessed, assessing): Teachers assess progress through regular
feedback.
5.     foster (fostered, fostered, fostering): Group projects foster teamwork and
communication.
6.     memorise (memorised, memorised, memorising): Rote learning encourages students to
memorise rather than understand.
7.     specialise (specialised, specialised, specialising): Undergraduates specialise in their
chosen field in later years.
8.     motivate (motivated, motivated, motivating): Skilled teachers motivate even reluctant
learners.
9.  broaden (broadened, broadened, broadening): Travel broadens young people’s
understanding of the world.
10. equip (equipped, equipped, equipping): Practical training equips graduates with job-
ready skills.

sections.title: Collocations and adjectives (10)
sections.content:
1.  higher education: Access to higher education has widened considerably. (Writing)
2.  critical thinking: Universities should develop students’ critical thinking. (Writing)
3.  well-rounded education: A well-rounded education includes arts as well as sciences.
(Writing)
4. lifelong learning: The modern economy demands lifelong learning. (Writing)
5. academic performance: Sleep has a direct effect on academic performance. (Writing)
6. student-centred: A student-centred approach places learners at the heart of the lesson.
(Writing)
7. compulsory education: Compulsory education should last until at least sixteen.
(Writing)
8. hands-on experience: Internships give students valuable hands-on experience.
(Speaking and Writing)
9. rote learning: Rote learning has limited long-term benefit. (Writing)
10. highly qualified: The school employs highly qualified teachers. (Speaking and Writing)

sections.title: Formal Task 2 collocations (5)
sections.content:
1.     lay the foundation for: Early schooling lays the foundation for later success.
2.     bridge the skills gap: Vocational courses help bridge the skills gap in industry.
3.     equip students with: Education should equip students with practical, transferable
skills.
4.     place emphasis on: Some systems place too much emphasis on examinations.
5.     broaden one’s horizons: Studying abroad can broaden a young person’s horizons.

sections.title: Speaking idioms and expressions (5)
sections.content:
1.     learn the ropes: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes at university. (Part 2)
2.     a steep learning curve: The first year of my degree was a steep learning curve. (Part 2)
3.     pass with flying colours: She passed her final exams with flying colours. (Part 1)
4.     hit the books: Before exams, I really have to hit the books. (Part 1)
5.     think outside the box: Good teachers encourage you to think outside the box. (Part 3)

sections.title: Part B
sections.content:
Exercise 4.2.1 · Vocabulary Match. Match each term (1 to 10) with its meaning (a to j).
1.     curriculum · 2. literacy · 3. assessment · 4. foster · 5. attainment · 6. vocation · 7. aptitude ·
8. cultivate · 9. compulsory · 10. broaden
a.     the ability to read and write
b.     required by law or rule
c.     a natural ability or talent
d.     the subjects taught in a course
e.     to encourage the development of something
f.     the level of success reached in learning
g.     a job or trade needing particular training
h.     to grow or develop a quality in someone
i.     the process of judging progress or ability
j.     to make something wider or more varied

1.     A well-rounded ______ develops both academic and creative abilities.
2.     Vocational training helps ______ the skills gap in many industries.
3.     Universities should focus on developing ______ thinking, not just memorisation.
4.     The modern economy increasingly demands ______ learning throughout one’s career.
5.     Early schooling lays the ______ for all later academic success.

1.     Do you think exams are the best way to assess students?
2.     How important is a university degree in today’s job market?
3.     Should schools focus more on practical skills or academic knowledge?

blocks.title: Technology and Automation

sections.title: Academic nouns (10)
sections.content:
1.  automation (স্বয়ংক্রিয়করণ): Automation has replaced many routine factory jobs.
2.  innovation (উদ্ভাবন): Constant innovation keeps the technology sector growing.
3.  connectivity (সংযোগ ব্যবস্থা): High-speed connectivity has transformed rural businesses.
4.  surveillance (নজরদারি): Digital surveillance raises serious concerns about privacy.
5.  algorithm (অ্যালগরিদম): Social media algorithms decide what users see.
6.  infrastructure (অবকাঠামো): Reliable digital infrastructure is now essential for the
economy.
7. obsolescence (অপ্রচলন): Rapid obsolescence forces consumers to replace devices often.
8. integration (সংহতকরণ): The integration of technology into classrooms is uneven.
9. artificial intelligence (কৃ ত্রিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা): Artificial intelligence is reshaping many
professions.
10. digital divide (ডিজিটাল বৈষম্য): The digital divide leaves poorer communities behind.

sections.content:

2. innovate (innovated, innovated, innovating): Companies that fail to innovate quickly

3. streamline (streamlined, streamlined, streamlining): New software has streamlined

4. integrate (integrated, integrated, integrating): Schools are integrating tablets into daily

5. revolutionise (revolutionised, revolutionised, revolutionising): The smartphone has
revolutionised communication.
6. facilitate (facilitated, facilitated, facilitating): Video calls facilitate remote

7. hack (hacked, hacked, hacking): Criminals can hack poorly protected networks.
8. upgrade (upgraded, upgraded, upgrading): Users must regularly upgrade their

9. disrupt (disrupted, disrupted, disrupting): Streaming services have disrupted the film
industry.
10. monitor (monitored, monitored, monitoring): Employers can monitor staff activity
online.

longer guarantees a well-paid job; employers increasingly value hands-on experience and

so the key is helping workers keep up with the times through retraining. - Q3: The internet has

however, it also demands strong digital literacy to separate reliable sources from
misinformation.

prevention is better than cure. - Q2: In many ways they are, because sedentary lifestyles and

Chapter 4 Batch 1 Answer Key
(For the final book, consolidate into Chapter 7. Placed here so the batch can be self-checked.
Speaking-drill answers are model responses; any natural, error-free answer using the target
vocabulary is acceptable.)
Topic 1: Environment
4.1.1 Match: 1-e, 2-a, 3-j, 4-b, 5-i, 6-c, 7-h, 8-d, 9-g, 10-f. 4.1.2 Completion: 1 strike, 2 pollutants,
3 renewable, 4 irreversible, 5 footprint. 4.1.3 Models. - Q1: Ordinary people can go green in
small ways, such as cutting their carbon footprint by using public transport, though individual
effort alone is only a drop in the ocean without industrial reform. - Q2: Individual effort
matters, but on its own it is a drop in the ocean; without governments taking collective action
and industries cutting emissions, personal choices cannot reverse the damage. - Q3: In future,
cities could become far greener by investing in public transport, expanding green spaces, and
adopting renewable energy, which together would shrink their carbon footprint.
Topic 2: Education
4.2.1 Match: 1-d, 2-a, 3-i, 4-e, 5-f, 6-g, 7-c, 8-h, 9-b, 10-j. 4.2.2 Completion: 1 education, 2 bridge,
3 critical, 4 lifelong, 5 foundation. 4.2.3 Models. - Q1: Exams measure knowledge under
pressure, but they reward rote learning over critical thinking, so continuous assessment often
gives a fairer picture of a student’s real attainment. - Q2: A degree still opens doors, but it no
longer guarantees a well-paid job; employers increasingly value hands-on experience and
transferable skills alongside academic attainment. - Q3: Ideally schools should do both, yet
many place too much emphasis on academic knowledge; teaching practical skills would equip
students far better for real life.
Topic 3: Technology
4.3.1 Match: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-e, 5-h, 6-i, 7-a, 8-f, 9-g, 10-j. 4.3.2 Completion: 1 transformed /
revolutionised, 2 automation, 3 digital, 4 concerns, 5 automated. 4.3.3 Models. - Q1: Technology
is a double-edged sword: information is now at our fingertips, which makes life easier, yet
many people end up glued to their screens, which complicates it. - Q2: It is a double-edged
sword: automation will render some routine jobs obsolete, but it should also create new roles,
so the key is helping workers keep up with the times through retraining. - Q3: The internet has
transformed the way people learn, since a wealth of information is now at our fingertips;
however, it also demands strong digital literacy to separate reliable sources from
misinformation.
Topic 4: Health
4.4.1 Match: 1-a, 2-c, 3-e, 4-d, 5-f, 6-g, 7-h, 8-i, 9-j, 10-b. 4.4.2 Completion: 1 balanced, 2 strain, 3
toll, 4 lifestyle, 5 alleviate. 4.4.3 Models. - Q1: Responsibility is shared: individuals must lead a
healthier lifestyle, but governments should promote a healthy lifestyle through education, since
prevention is better than cure. - Q2: In many ways they are, because sedentary lifestyles and
fast food have become the norm; that said, medical advances mean people also live longer, so it
is a mixed picture. - Q3: People can be encouraged to eat healthily through public campaigns,
clearer food labelling, and making nutritious food more affordable, since prevention is better
than cure.
Topic 5: Crime
4.5.1 Match: 1-c, 2-f, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d, 6-g, 7-i, 8-j, 9-e, 10-h. 4.5.2 Completion: 1 deterrent, 2
rehabilitate, 3 causes, 4 impose, 5 reintegrate. 4.5.3 Models. - Q1: Prison can act as a deterrent,
but on its own it does little to lower recidivism; programmes that rehabilitate offenders and
help them turn over a new leaf tend to work better in the long run. - Q2: The causes are largely
social; crime often stems from poverty and a lack of opportunity, so addressing the root causes
tends to be more effective than harsh punishment alone. - Q3: For minor offences, community
service is often preferable, because it helps offenders reintegrate into society and turn over a
new leaf rather than hardening them behind bars.

Arts and Heritage, and Media and Advertising.
Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 2 of 3)
This batch covers domains six to ten: Globalisation and Cultural Assimilation, Urbanisation and
Infrastructure, Business and Economy, Arts and Heritage, and Media and Advertising. The
format is identical to Batch 1. Work each topic, then complete its three exercises before
checking the key at the end of the file. Keep the formal Task 2 collocations and the Speaking
idioms apart in your mind; the strict register rule that governs them is the whole subject of
Chapter 5.
Topic 6: Globalisation and Cultural Assimilation
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
1.  globalisation (বিশ্বায়ন): Globalisation has linked distant economies more closely than
ever.
2. assimilation (আত্তীকরণ): The assimilation of immigrants raises questions about cultural
identity.
3. homogenisation (সমরূপীকরণ): Critics warn of the homogenisation of world cultures.
4. diversity (বৈচিত্র্য): Cultural diversity enriches modern cities.
5. heritage (ঐতিহ্য): Migration can dilute a community’s cultural heritage.
6. identity (পরিচয়): Young people often struggle to protect their national identity abroad.
7. multiculturalism (বহুসংস্কৃ তিবাদ): Multiculturalism has become a defining feature of large
cities.
8. interdependence (পারস্পরিক নির্ভরশীলতা): Global interdependence makes isolation almost
impossible.
9. migration (অভিবাসন): Mass migration reshapes both host and home countries.
10. westernisation (পাশ্চাত্যকরণ): Rapid westernisation worries many traditional societies.
Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
1.  integrate (integrated, integrated, integrating): Immigrants who integrate quickly tend
to prosper.
2. assimilate (assimilated, assimilated, assimilating): Some minorities are pressured to
assimilate into the majority culture.
3. adapt (adapted, adapted, adapting): Newcomers must adapt to unfamiliar customs.
4. preserve (preserved, preserved, preserving): Diaspora communities work hard to
preserve their traditions.
5. erode (eroded, eroded, eroding): Foreign media can slowly erode local values.
6. embrace (embraced, embraced, embracing): Younger generations tend to embrace
global culture.
7. exchange (exchanged, exchanged, exchanging): Nations exchange ideas as freely as
goods.
8. dominate (dominated, dominated, dominating): A handful of languages dominate the
internet.
9. dilute (diluted, diluted, diluting): Globalisation may dilute distinctive local customs.
10. migrate (migrated, migrated, migrating): Millions migrate each year in search of work.

2.     global marketplace: Small firms can now reach the global marketplace. (Writing)

4.     loss of identity: Rapid change can lead to a loss of identity. (Writing)
5.  cultural exchange: Tourism promotes valuable cultural exchange. (Writing)

(Writing)

Writing)

3.     a sense of belonging: A shared culture gives people a sense of belonging.

between nations.

Topic 7: Urbanisation and Infrastructure
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
1.     urbanisation (নগরায়ন): Rapid urbanisation has strained city services.
2.     infrastructure (অবকাঠামো): Reliable infrastructure underpins economic growth.
3.     congestion (যানজট): Traffic congestion wastes both time and fuel.
4.     overpopulation (জনাধিক্য): Overpopulation intensifies competition for housing.
5.     sanitation (পয়ঃনিষ্কাশন): Poor sanitation spreads disease in dense slums.
6.     slum (বস্তি): Millions live in overcrowded urban slums.
7.     amenities (সুযোগ-সুবিধা): New suburbs often lack basic amenities.
8.     housing (আবাসন): Affordable housing is scarce in major cities.
9.     relocation (স্থানান্তর): The relocation of factories reshaped the local economy.
10.    urban sprawl (নগরের অপরিকল্পিত বিস্তার): Unchecked urban sprawl consumes farmland.
Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
1.     urbanise (urbanised, urbanised, urbanising): Developing nations are urbanising at
record speed.
2.     migrate (migrated, migrated, migrating): Rural workers migrate to cities for jobs.
3.     commute (commuted, commuted, commuting): Millions commute long distances each
day.
4.     expand (expanded, expanded, expanding): Cities expand outward as populations grow.
5.     congest (congested, congested, congesting): Too many vehicles congest the main roads.
6.     accommodate (accommodated, accommodated, accommodating): Cities struggle to
accommodate new arrivals.
7.     relocate (relocated, relocated, relocating): Some residents were forced to relocate.
8.     modernise (modernised, modernised, modernising): The government is modernising
the rail network.
9.  deteriorate (deteriorated, deteriorated, deteriorating): Ageing infrastructure continues
to deteriorate.
10. develop (developed, developed, developing): Planners must develop new residential
areas carefully.
Collocations and adjectives (10)
1.  traffic congestion: Traffic congestion is worsening in most capitals. (Writing)
2.  affordable housing: A shortage of affordable housing pushes prices up. (Writing)
3.  public transport: Efficient public transport reduces reliance on cars. (Speaking and
Writing)
4. rapid urbanisation: Rapid urbanisation outpaces infrastructure. (Writing)
5. densely populated: Densely populated districts face constant pressure. (Writing)
6. urban planning: Sound urban planning prevents future problems. (Writing)
7. rural-urban migration: Rural-urban migration drives city growth. (Writing)
8. overcrowded: Public hospitals are dangerously overcrowded. (Speaking and Writing)
9. green spaces: Green spaces improve residents’ wellbeing. (Writing)
10. cost of living: The rising cost of living forces families to the outskirts. (Speaking and
Writing)
Formal Task 2 collocations (5)
1.     put pressure on public services: Rapid growth puts pressure on public services.
2.     ease traffic congestion: Better transport links can ease traffic congestion.
3.     cope with rapid growth: Many cities cannot cope with rapid growth.
4.     a shortage of affordable housing: There is a chronic shortage of affordable housing.
5.     improve the standard of living: Investment in infrastructure improves the standard
of living.
Speaking idioms and expressions (5)
1.     the hustle and bustle: I love the hustle and bustle of city life. (Part 2)
2.     a concrete jungle: The centre has become a concrete jungle. (Part 3)
3.     the rat race: Many people want to escape the rat race. (Part 3)
4.     a stone’s throw away: The station is just a stone’s throw away. (Part 1)

Topic 9: Arts, Heritage and Tradition
Part A

10.    masterpiece (অনবদ্য সৃষ্টি): The painting is regarded as a masterpiece.

Topic 10: Media, Mass Communication and Advertising
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
1.     propaganda (অপপ্রচার): Wartime propaganda shaped public feeling.

Chapter 4 Batch 2 Answer Key
(For the final book, consolidate into Chapter 7. Speaking-drill answers are model responses; any

Topic 6: Globalisation
4.6.1 Match: 1-c, 2-i, 3-b, 4-f, 5-e, 6-g, 7-d, 8-j, 9-a, 10-h. 4.6.2 Completion: 1 erode, 2 diversity, 3
assimilate / integrate, 4 barriers, 5 risk. 4.6.3 Models. - Q1: Globalisation has been a mixed
blessing: it has connected us to a global marketplace and fostered mutual understanding, yet it
also risks eroding traditional values, so the world can feel both closer together and worlds
apart. - Q2: To some extent, yes; global media can erode traditional values and homogenise
cultures, though many communities work hard to keep their traditions alive. - Q3: People can
protect their traditions by passing them down from generation to generation, celebrating
festivals, and teaching their language, all of which keep a strong sense of identity alive.
Topic 7: Urbanisation
4.7.1 Match: 1-c, 2-b, 3-a, 4-d, 5-f, 6-e, 7-g, 8-h, 9-i, 10-j. 4.7.2 Completion: 1 urbanisation, 2
affordable, 3 congestion, 4 cope, 5 planning. 4.7.3 Models. - Q1: Rapid growth puts pressure on
public services and worsens traffic congestion, and a shortage of affordable housing pushes
many families to the outskirts, turning some districts into a concrete jungle. - Q2: I prefer the
city, mainly for the amenities and opportunities, even if it means putting up with the hustle
and bustle; the countryside is calmer, but it can feel like the middle of nowhere. - Q3:
Governments can make cities more liveable through sound urban planning, affordable housing,
reliable public transport, and more green spaces to offset the concrete jungle.
Topic 8: Business and Economy
4.8.1 Match: 1-c, 2-e, 3-a, 4-d, 5-b, 6-h, 7-f, 8-g, 9-j, 10-i. 4.8.2 Completion: 1 stimulate, 2 widen,
3 inflation, 4 create, 5 economy. 4.8.3 Models. - Q1: Money matters, but it is not the only
measure of success; a person who climbs the career ladder while struggling to make ends meet
may be far less content than someone with modest means and a fulfilling life. - Q2: Yes, I think
so; unregulated markets tend to widen the gap between rich and poor, so governments should
invest in public services and use fair taxation to support those struggling to make ends meet. -
Q3: It depends on the person; working for a company offers stability, whereas being self-
employed offers freedom, so it is really about which side of that trade-off suits you.
Topic 9: Arts and Heritage
4.9.1 Match: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d, 5-e, 6-g, 7-f, 8-h, 9-i, 10-j. 4.9.2 Completion: 1 generations, 2
identity, 3 down, 4 traditions, 5 reflects. 4.9.3 Models. - Q1: Protecting traditional culture
matters because it instils a sense of identity and offers a window into the past; customs that
stand the test of time connect each generation to the one before it. - Q2: To a certain extent, yes;
the fast pace of modern life pushes some customs aside, but renewed interest in heritage means
many traditions still stand the test of time. - Q3: I believe they should; public funding sustains
the arts, which are an integral part of a nation’s identity and offer a window into its history
that the market alone would not preserve.
Topic 10: Media and Advertising
4.10.1 Match: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-f, 5-h, 6-a, 7-e, 8-g, 9-j, 10-i. 4.10.2 Completion: 1 shape, 2
manipulate, 3 spread, 4 account, 5 advertising. 4.10.3 Models. - Q1: Advertising certainly has
too much influence, since clever campaigns manipulate consumer behaviour and encourage
people to jump on the bandwagon of every trend, though a discerning viewer learns to take
such messages with a pinch of salt. - Q2: Not entirely; much online content is biased or
sensationalised, and misinformation spreads like wildfire, so it is wise to take what you read
with a pinch of salt and check reliable sources. - Q3: Social media has transformed how we get
information, since breaking news now travels in seconds; the downside is that it also lets
rumours spread unchecked.
End of Chapter 4, Batch 2. Batch 3 covers Government and Public Spending, Transportation,
Youth and Family, Scientific Research, and Tourism and Travel.
Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 3 of 3)
This final batch covers the last five domains: Government Governance and Public Spending,
Transportation and Mobility, Youth and Family and Generational Gaps, Scientific Research and
Innovation, and International Tourism and Travel. Complete each topic and its three exercises
before checking the key at the end. With this batch, all fifteen IELTS domains are covered.
Topic 11: Government Governance and Public Spending
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
1.     governance (শাসন ব্যবস্থা): Good governance depends on transparency and accountability.
2.     legislation (আইন প্রণয়ন): New legislation was passed to curb pollution.
3.     bureaucracy (আমলাতন্ত্র): Excessive bureaucracy slows down public services.
4.     subsidy (ভর্তুকি): Fuel subsidies keep transport affordable for the poor.
5.     taxation (করারোপ): Progressive taxation redistributes wealth.
6.     accountability (জবাবদিহিতা): Voters demand greater accountability from officials.
7.     welfare (জনকল্যাণ): The welfare system supports the unemployed.
8.     expenditure (ব্যয়): Public expenditure on health has risen steadily.
9.     transparency (স্বচ্ছতা): Transparency reduces the scope for corruption.
10.    policy (নীতি): Sound economic policy underpins stable growth.
Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
1.     allocate (allocated, allocated, allocating): The budget allocates more to education this
year.
2.     implement (implemented, implemented, implementing): Governments must
implement reforms carefully.
3.     regulate (regulated, regulated, regulating): Agencies regulate food safety and drug
quality.
4.     subsidise (subsidised, subsidised, subsidising): The state subsidises public transport.
5.     legislate (legislated, legislated, legislating): Parliament legislated against child labour.
6.     govern (governed, governed, governing): A stable coalition now governs the country.
7.  impose (imposed, imposed, imposing): The government imposed a tax on sugary
drinks.
8. prioritise (prioritised, prioritised, prioritising): Officials must prioritise essential
services.
9. fund (funded, funded, funding): The state fully funds primary schooling.
10. reform (reformed, reformed, reforming): The new minister pledged to reform the tax
system.
Collocations and adjectives (10)
1.  public spending: Public spending on healthcare must rise. (Writing)
2.  tax revenue: Tax revenue funds essential services. (Writing)
3.  welfare state: The welfare state protects the most vulnerable. (Writing)
4.  government intervention: Government intervention is sometimes unavoidable.
(Writing)
5. fiscal policy: Sound fiscal policy controls inflation. (Writing)
6. red tape: Businesses complain about excessive red tape. (Speaking and Writing)
7. accountable to the public: Officials must remain accountable to the public. (Writing)
8. public services: Reliable public services improve daily life. (Speaking and Writing)
9. state-funded: State-funded universities widen access. (Writing)
10. budget deficit: A large budget deficit limits future spending. (Writing)

2.     prioritise public spending: Authorities must prioritise public spending on essentials.
3.     hold the government accountable: Free elections hold the government accountable.
4.     impose higher taxes: One option is to impose higher taxes on the wealthy.
5.     invest in public services: Investing in public services benefits everyone.
Speaking idioms and expressions (5)

2.     tighten the purse strings: In a downturn, the government tightens the purse strings.
(Part 3)
3.     call the shots: In the end, elected leaders should call the shots. (Part 3)
4.     for the greater good: Some sacrifices are made for the greater good. (Part 3)
5.     cut through the red tape: We need to cut through the red tape to speed things up.
(Part 3)

Topic 12: Transportation and Mobility
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
1.     mobility (গতিশীলতা): Affordable transport improves social mobility.
2.     commuter (নিত্যযাত্রী): Daily commuters face long, crowded journeys.
3.     fare (ভাড়া): Rising fares discourage the use of public transport.
4.     logistics (সরবরাহ ব্যবস্থাপনা): Efficient logistics keep goods moving.
5.     gridlock (তীব্র যানজট): Morning gridlock paralyses the city centre.
6.     pedestrian (পথচারী): Wider pavements make streets safer for pedestrians.
7.     fuel (জ্বালানি): Higher fuel prices raise the cost of everything.
8.     emission (নিঃসরণ): Vehicle emissions are a major source of urban pollution.
9.     congestion (যানজট): Congestion charges aim to reduce city traffic.
10.    transit (গণপরিবহন): A modern transit system eases pressure on roads.
Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
1.     commute (commuted, commuted, commuting): Thousands commute into the city each
morning.
2.  transport (transported, transported, transporting): Trains transport goods more
cheaply than trucks.
3. congest (congested, congested, congesting): Private cars congest the narrow roads.
4. navigate (navigated, navigated, navigating): Cyclists navigate busy streets daily.
5. emit (emitted, emitted, emitting): Older buses emit far more pollution.
6. relieve (relieved, relieved, relieving): A new bypass relieved chronic congestion.
7. expand (expanded, expanded, expanding): The city plans to expand its metro line.
8. connect (connected, connected, connecting): The bridge connects two remote districts.
9. upgrade (upgraded, upgraded, upgrading): Authorities are upgrading the rail network.
10. deter (deterred, deterred, deterring): High parking fees deter car use.
Collocations and adjectives (10)
1.  mass transit: An efficient mass transit system reduces car dependence. (Writing)
2.  traffic jam: I was stuck in a traffic jam for an hour. (Speaking)
3.  rush hour: Roads are gridlocked at rush hour. (Speaking and Writing)
4.  carbon emissions: Electric buses cut carbon emissions sharply. (Writing)
5.  congestion charge: The congestion charge reduced city-centre traffic. (Writing)
6.  eco-friendly transport: Cycling is the most eco-friendly transport of all. (Writing)
7.  road network: A dense road network supports trade. (Writing)

(Writing)

Chapter 4 Batch 3 Answer Key
(For the final book, consolidate into Chapter 7. Speaking-drill answers are model responses; any

Topic 11: Government and Public Spending
4.11.1 Match: 1-c, 2-e, 3-b, 4-f, 5-d, 6-a, 7-h, 8-g, 9-i, 10-j. 4.11.2 Completion: 1 allocate, 2
accountable, 3 services, 4 red, 5 policy. 4.11.3 Models. - Q1: Governments should prioritise
public spending on essentials such as healthcare and education, since simply throwing money
at less urgent projects rarely serves the greater good. - Q2: I think they are fair, within reason;
the wealthy can afford to contribute more, and that revenue can fund public services, though
taxes should not be so high that they discourage enterprise. - Q3: Governments can curb
corruption through greater transparency, strict accountability, and cutting through the red
tape that gives officials room to abuse the system.
Topic 12: Transportation
4.12.1 Match: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b, 5-e, 6-f, 7-g, 8-h, 9-i, 10-j. 4.12.2 Completion: 1 invest, 2
discourage, 3 reduce, 4 transit / mass transit, 5 connectivity. 4.12.3 Models. - Q1: Congestion
can be eased by investing in mass transit and introducing congestion charges to discourage
private car use; otherwise cities simply grind to a halt at rush hour. - Q2: More often than not,
yes; many people reach for the car out of habit even for short trips, which leaves roads bumper
to bumper and worsens emissions. - Q3: Public transport would attract more users if it were
cheaper, more frequent, and better connected, so that commuters saw it as a genuine
alternative rather than a last resort.
Topic 13: Youth and Family
4.13.1 Match: 1-b, 2-a, 3-f, 4-d, 5-e, 6-g, 7-h, 8-i, 9-j, 10-c. 4.13.2 Completion: 1 gap, 2 values, 3
balance, 4 shape, 5 time. 4.13.3 Models. - Q1: The generation gap does feel wider today, largely
because technology moves so fast that parents and teenagers do not always see eye to eye,
though open conversation can still bridge it. - Q2: Both matter, but as children grow, peer
pressure often outweighs parental guidance; even so, parents remain the first role models and
shape a child’s core values. - Q3: There are trade-offs either way; a large family offers close-knit
support, whereas a small one may allow more quality time and resources per child, so neither is
simply better.
Topic 14: Scientific Research
4.14.1 Match: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-e, 5-c, 6-h, 7-i, 8-j, 9-f, 10-g. 4.14.2 Completion: 1 boundaries, 2
rigorous, 3 questions / concerns, 4 funding, 5 pave. 4.14.3 Models. - Q1: Governments should
fund scientific research generously, because pushing the boundaries of knowledge through trial
and error paves the way for the breakthroughs that improve everyday life. - Q2: Not
necessarily; while most research pushes the boundaries of knowledge for the better, some
advances raise serious ethical questions, so progress needs to go hand in hand with careful
regulation. - Q3: For me, the smartphone is the standout; it put a wealth of information at our
fingertips and, for better or worse, has been a genuine game changer in daily life.
Topic 15: Tourism and Travel
4.15.1 Match: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d, 5-f, 6-e, 7-h, 8-i, 9-j, 10-g. 4.15.2 Completion: 1 boost, 2 broaden,
3 strain, 4 preserve, 5 cultural. 4.15.3 Models. - Q1: International travel has boomed because it
broadens people’s horizons and offers a welcome change of scenery; once you catch the travel
bug, exploring new destinations becomes hard to resist. - Q2: It does both; tourism can boost
the local economy and promote cultural understanding, yet mass tourism puts a strain on local
resources and can degrade the very attractions people come to see. - Q3: I lean toward
independent travel, because it lets you get off the beaten track and immerse yourself in local
life, though a package holiday is more convenient if you are short on time.

Chapter 4: Topic-Based Lexical Mastery (Batch 1 of 3)
The fifteen domains in this chapter are the topics IELTS returns to again and again. Whatever
the exact question, your Task 2 essay and your Speaking answers will draw on this vocabulary.
Each topic gives you a complete bundle: ten academic nouns, ten precise verbs, ten collocations
and adjectives, five formal collocations built for Writing Task 2, and five natural idioms built
for Speaking. The line between the last two matters enormously, and Chapter 5 is devoted to it;
here, simply notice that the formal set is labelled for Writing and the idiom set for Speaking,
and keep them apart.
This batch covers the first five domains: Environment, Education, Technology, Health, and
Crime. Batches 2 and 3 cover the remaining ten. Work each topic, then do its three exercises
before checking the key at the end of the file.
A note on the Bangla glosses: they give the everyday meaning of each academic noun so the
term is anchored to something you already know. Do not translate word for word into your
essays; use the English term in its natural collocation.



Topic 1: Environment and Climate Shift
Part A
Academic nouns (10)
  1.     emission (নিঃসরণ): Industrial emissions are a leading driver of global warming.
  2.     deforestation (বন উজাড় ): Widespread deforestation has accelerated the loss of natural
         habitats.
  3.     biodiversity (জীববৈচিত্র্য): The destruction of wetlands threatens the region’s biodiversity.
  4.     ecosystem (বাস্তু তন্ত্র): Even small changes in temperature can disrupt a fragile ecosystem.
  5.     degradation (অবক্ষয়): Soil degradation reduces agricultural productivity over time.
  6.     sustainability (টেকসইতা): Long-term sustainability must guide national energy policy.
  7.     conservation (সংরক্ষণ): The conservation of freshwater resources is now an urgent
         priority.
  8.     pollutant (দূষক): Vehicle exhaust releases harmful pollutants into the atmosphere.
  9.     depletion (নিঃশেষ হওয়া): The depletion of fossil fuels has intensified the search for
         alternatives.

  10. carbon footprint (কার্বন পদচিহ্ন): Individuals can reduce their carbon footprint by using
      public transport.
Precise verbs (10), forms shown as (past, participle, -ing)
  1.  emit (emitted, emitted, emitting): Factories emit large quantities of greenhouse gases.
  2.  deplete (depleted, depleted, depleting): Overfishing has depleted marine stocks
      worldwide.
  3. mitigate (mitigated, mitigated, mitigating): Reforestation can mitigate the effects of
      climate change.
  4. conserve (conserved, conserved, conserving): Households should conserve water
      during the dry season.
  5. pollute (polluted, polluted, polluting): Untreated waste continues to pollute major
      rivers.
  6. degrade (degraded, degraded, degrading): Intensive farming gradually degrades the
      soil.
  7. offset (offset, offset, offsetting): Companies can offset emissions by funding tree
      planting.
  8. preserve (preserved, preserved, preserving): Protected areas help preserve endangered
      species.
  9. exploit (exploited, exploited, exploiting): Nations must stop exploiting natural
      resources recklessly.
  10. contaminate (contaminated, contaminated, contaminating): Chemical runoff can
      contaminate groundwater.
Collocations and adjectives (10)
  1.  renewable energy: Investment in renewable energy is rising steadily. (Writing)
  2.  fossil fuels: We remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. (Writing)
  3.  environmentally friendly: Many consumers now prefer environmentally friendly
      products. (Speaking and Writing)
  4. a pressing environmental concern: Air quality has become a pressing environmental
      concern. (Writing)
  5. greenhouse gas emissions: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires global
      cooperation. (Writing)
  6. irreversible damage: Rising sea levels could cause irreversible damage to coastlines.
      (Writing)
  7. carbon neutral: Several cities aim to become carbon neutral by 2050. (Writing)
  8. finite resources: Water and oil are finite resources that must be managed carefully.
      (Writing)
  9. eco-friendly (Speaking): I try to make eco-friendly choices, like carrying a reusable
      bottle. (Speaking)
  10. climate change (adjective use, climate-related): Climate-related disasters are becoming
      more frequent. (Writing)
Formal Task 2 collocations (5)

  1.     pose a serious threat to: Rising temperatures pose a serious threat to food security.
  2.     at the expense of: Economic growth should not come at the expense of the
         environment.
  3.     strike a balance between: Governments must strike a balance between development
         and conservation.
  4.     have a detrimental impact on: Plastic waste has a detrimental impact on marine life.
  5.     take collective action: Only collective action can address the climate crisis effectively.
Speaking idioms and expressions (5)
  1.     a drop in the ocean: Recycling at home helps, but it is a drop in the ocean compared
         with industry. (Part 3)
  2.     the tip of the iceberg: The visible pollution is just the tip of the iceberg. (Part 3)
  3.     go green: More families are trying to go green these days. (Part 1)
  4.     weather the storm: Coastal communities have to weather the storm of frequent
         flooding. (Part 3)
  5.     a breath of fresh air: Escaping to the countryside is a real breath of fresh air. (Part 2)

Part B
Exercise 4.1.1 · Vocabulary Match. Match each term (1 to 10) with its meaning (a to j).
  1.     emission · 2. biodiversity · 3. depletion · 4. mitigate · 5. sustainability · 6. pollutant · 7. offset
         · 8. finite · 9. conservation · 10. degrade
  a.     the variety of living things in an area
  b.     to reduce the severity of something harmful
  c.     a substance that makes air, water, or soil dirty
  d.     limited in quantity, not endless
  e.     the release of gas or heat into the air
  f.     to make something worse in quality over time
  g.     the careful protection of natural resources
  h.     to balance out a negative amount with a positive action
  i.     the state of being able to continue over the long term
  j.     the using up or reduction of a resource
Exercise 4.1.2 · Essay Sentence Completion. Complete each Task 2 sentence with a term from
this topic.

         protection.
  2.     Burning fossil fuels releases harmful ______ into the atmosphere.
  3.     Investment in ______ energy is essential if we are to cut emissions.
  4.     Deforestation causes ______ damage that cannot be undone.
  5.     Individuals can lower their carbon ______ by choosing public transport.

Exercise 4.1.3 · Speaking Simulation Drill. Answer each Part 3 question in two to three
sentences, using at least one target idiom and one collocation.
  1.     What can ordinary people do to protect the environment?
  2.     Do you think individual effort is enough to solve climate change?
  3.     How might cities become more environmentally friendly in the future?


Topic 2: Education and Pedagogy
